title: Champagne
description: A cold, chalky corner of northern France that turned a winemaking problem into the world's most famous sparkling wine.
L: Champagne lies about 150 km north-east of Paris, at around 49 degrees north, near the northern limit for ripening grapes. Average temperatures are around 11 degrees Celsius. Grapes ripen just enough, giving high acidity and low sugar: poor still wine, but perfect base wine for sparkling. The appellation covers about 34,000 hectares.

Champagne's soils are chalk, often under a thin topsoil. Chalk drains well yet holds water like a sponge, feeding vines in dry summers. It reflects light and heat. The Romans dug chalk pits, crayères, that houses later used as cellars: Reims and Épernay have hundreds of kilometres of tunnels at a steady 10 to 12 degrees.
Why is Champagne's chalk so valuable?
It drains well yet stores water, and its cellars stay cool
Chalk regulates water, and its tunnels make ideal cellars.

In Champagne's cold winters, fermentation often stopped and restarted in spring, making wine fizzy by accident. The English, in the 17th century, bottled it in stronger glass and enjoyed the bubbles. Dom Pérignon, a monk at Hautvillers, didn't invent sparkling wine, but he improved blending and pressing. Houses developed the method in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Not true. He improved blending and pressing, but bubbles came from accidental refermentation, and the English first bottled it as sparkling.
Champagne is cold, giving high-acid base wine
Chalk regulates water and provides cool cellars
Bubbles began as an accident; houses refined the method
Name the main areas for each

Pinot Noir is about 38% of plantings, Meunier about 31%, Chardonnay about 31%. Pinot Noir gives body, structure and red fruit; Meunier gives fruit and roundness; Chardonnay gives finesse, acidity and ageing potential. Four other grapes, like Arbane and Petit Meslier, are allowed but rare.

The Montagne de Reims, with Grand Crus like Aÿ, Bouzy and Verzenay, favours Pinot Noir. The Vallée de la Marne, with frost pockets and clay, suits late-budding Meunier. The Côte des Blancs, on pure chalk, with Cramant, Avize and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, is Chardonnay country. The Côte des Bar, in the south, on Kimmeridgian marl, grows mainly Pinot Noir.
Montagne, Vallée, Côte des Blancs, Côte des Bar
Match each area to its main grape.
Blanc de Blancs is made only from white grapes, usually Chardonnay; Blanc de Noirs only from black grapes, Pinot Noir and Meunier.
Which grape brings finesse and ageing potential to Champagne?
Chardonnay gives acidity, finesse and longevity.
Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay are Champagne's grapes
Blanc de Blancs and Blanc de Noirs use only one colour
Put the steps of the traditional method in order

Grapes are hand-picked and pressed whole and gently. The base wines are fermented, then blended, often with reserve wines from earlier years. The blend is bottled with sugar and yeast, the liqueur de tirage, and sealed with a crown cap. A second fermentation in the bottle creates about 6 atmospheres of pressure.

The wine then ages on its lees, dead yeast: at least 15 months for non-vintage, at least 3 years for vintage. Autolysis adds brioche, biscuit and nutty notes. Riddling moves the yeast to the neck. Disgorgement freezes the neck and removes the plug. Dosage, wine with sugar, tops up the bottle before corking.
Put the traditional method steps in order.
Add sugar and yeast, and seal
Each step builds on the one before.

Champagne requires hand harvesting. Whole bunches are pressed gently, so black grapes give white juice without colour or bitterness. Pressing is limited: from 4,000 kg of grapes, only 2,550 litres of juice may be used. The first 2,050 litres, the cuvée, are the finest; the next 500, the taille, are fruitier.
What is the minimum lees ageing for non-vintage Champagne?
Non-vintage needs 15 months in total, with at least 12 on lees; vintage needs 3 years.
Champagne's second fermentation happens in the bottle
Hand-picking and gentle pressing give white juice
Explain the role of the houses

Large houses, or maisons, like Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Bollinger and Krug, own some vineyards but buy most grapes from about 16,000 growers. They blend across villages and years for a consistent house style, especially in non-vintage. Houses make about two-thirds of Champagne's sales.

Growers who make and sell their own Champagne are called récoltant-manipulants, labelled RM. Since the 1990s, grower Champagne has become popular for showing a single village or vineyard. Co-operatives, CM, pool members' grapes. Label codes tell you who made the wine.
RM grower; NM house; CM co-op
Match each label code to its meaning.
The small code on the label reveals the producer type.

Champagne's villages were once ranked on a scale, the échelle des crus, which set grape prices: 17 villages were Grand Cru, 100%, and 42 Premier Cru, 90 to 99%. The price system ended in 2010, but the names still appear on labels.
Most Champagne is sold by large houses that buy grapes.
Yes. Houses account for about two-thirds of sales.
Houses blend grapes from many growers for a house style
Grower Champagne, RM, shows single villages
Explain non-vintage, vintage and prestige cuvée

Dosage, added after disgorgement, sets the sweetness. Brut Nature: 0 to 3 g/l, no sugar added. Extra Brut: up to 6. Brut, the most common: up to 12. Extra Dry: 12 to 17. Sec: 17 to 32. Demi-Sec: 32 to 50. Doux: over 50. Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, a common confusion.

Non-vintage, NV, blends several years for consistency, about 80% of production. Vintage comes from one exceptional year, aged at least 3 years. Prestige cuvées, like Dom Pérignon, Cristal or Krug Grande Cuvée, are a house's top wine. Rosé is made by blending a little still red wine, unusually allowed in Champagne, or by saignée.
Order these Champagne styles from driest to sweetest.
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut.

Many producers now print the disgorgement date. A recently disgorged wine is fresher; one disgorged years ago has developed more toast and nuttiness. Some houses, like Bollinger with its R.D., release wines disgorged after very long lees ageing.
How is most rosé Champagne made?
By blending in a little still red wine
Champagne is an exception that allows blending red into white.
Dosage terms run from Brut Nature to Doux
NV, vintage and prestige cuvée are the main categories
Rosé Champagne is usually blended with red wine
Reading Champagne and eating with it

A Champagne label shows the house or grower, the sweetness level, the producer code, NV or a vintage, and sometimes Grand Cru, Premier Cru, Blanc de Blancs or Blanc de Noirs. The word Champagne itself is protected: only wine from the region made by the traditional method can use it.

Serve at 8 to 10 degrees; vintage and prestige cuvées a little warmer. A white wine glass shows the aromas better than a narrow flute. Open by holding the cork and turning the bottle slowly, letting the pressure out with a sigh, not a pop.
8 to 10 degrees, in a wine glass
Why might a white wine glass suit Champagne better than a flute?
It lets aromas gather and show
A wider bowl reveals the wine's aromas.

Brut Champagne suits oysters, caviar, sushi, fried food and salty snacks; acidity and bubbles cut fat and salt. Blanc de Blancs suits shellfish; Blanc de Noirs and rosé suit poultry, salmon and charcuterie. Vintage and aged Champagne suit truffle and roast chicken. Demi-Sec suits fruit desserts.
Sweet cake makes Brut taste sour; choose Demi-Sec.
Labels show producer, dosage, code and vintage
Serve at 8 to 10 degrees in a wine glass
Brut suits oysters and fried food; Demi-Sec suits desserts
Describe Champagne's climate, chalk and grapes
Match each area to its grape.
What is the minimum ageing for vintage Champagne?
Extra Dry Champagne is drier than Brut.
Not true. Extra Dry, 12 to 17 g/l, is sweeter than Brut.
A grower who makes their own Champagne uses the code ____.
Champagne is cold and chalky, giving high-acid base wine
Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay are its grapes
The traditional method and lees ageing create its style
Labels show dosage, producer type and vintage
